claims.text: A CrCoNi-based alloy can initially exist as a homogenized, random FCC solid solution.
Controlled metastable nanoclusters govern toughness retention in FCC high-entropy alloys.
Metastable nanoclusters facilitate favorable dislocation slip.
Metastable nanoclusters promote crack bridging and crack deflection.
Excessive grain-boundary nanosegregation causes interfacial decohesion.
Grain-boundary decohesion triggers premature crack initiation and toughness loss.
An intermediate-temperature heat treatment at approximately 600–800 °C can trigger metastable local ordering or nanocluster formation.
A suitably tuned heat treatment can form beneficial particles or local order without producing detrimental grain-boundary segregation.
L12-type precipitates or controlled grain-boundary segregations can mediate transformation-induced toughening.
Transformation of metastable particles can increase toughness through crack deflection, crack bridging, and crack-tip shielding.
CrCoNi has an FCC solid-solution state with an energetically competitive HCP state, enabling a dislocation-associated FCC-to-HCP transformation.
The optimized heat treatment will increase fracture toughness relative to a homogenized baseline.
The optimized heat treatment will increase ductility relative to a homogenized baseline.
Extending the heat treatment sufficiently to produce pronounced grain-boundary nanosegregation will reduce toughness.
The proposed behavior applies to metastable high-entropy alloys with FCC matrices under moderate heat-treatment temperatures and standard deformation rates.
Alloys with fundamentally different crystal structures or subjected to extreme temperatures may not follow the proposed mechanism.
A treatment atmosphere should be inert to prevent oxidation from confounding the mechanical response.
Failure of the optimized-treatment specimens to show a statistically significant toughness and ductility improvement over the homogenized baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
